title: Pâte à Choux Recipe (Foolproof Choux Pastry for Cream Puffs + Gougères)

blocks.text: Quick Overview

items: Prep time: 15 minutes
Cook time: 25–30 minutes
Total time: 40–45 minutes
Yield: about 30 medium puffs

blocks.text: Why This Is a Date-Night Power Move
Pâte à choux is one of those “looks like you know what you’re doing” doughs. You make it once, pipe a few puffs, and suddenly dessert feels like it came from a pastry shop.

It’s not just dessert energy. It’s *competence* energy. This dough is the foundation for cream puffs, éclairs, profiteroles, Paris–Brest rings, and even savory gougères. If you can nail this, you’ve basically unlocked a whole wing of the French bakery.
And if you’re cooking for a date, this is the kind of thing that gets you that look across the table that says, “Okay… so you *do* have range.”
What Is Pâte à Choux?
Pâte à choux (pronounced “pat-ah-shoo”) is a light pastry dough that’s cooked twice.

items: First, you cook the dough on the stovetop to create a smooth paste (called the *panade*).
Then, you bake it so the moisture turns into steam, which inflates the dough into a hollow, crisp shell.

blocks.text: No yeast. No baking powder. Just technique.
Ingredients

items: 113 g water
113 g whole milk
113 g unsalted butter, cut into 1/2-inch pieces
12 g granulated sugar
3 g kosher salt (about 3/4 teaspoon)
140 g bread flour
225 g eggs (4 to 5 large eggs), lightly beaten

blocks.text: Ingredient Notes (So You Don’t Overthink It)

items: **Water + milk:** Water gives you better puff and structure. Milk gives you flavor and nicer browning. This half-and-half situation is the sweet spot.
**Butter:** This is your flavor base. Use unsalted so you control the salt.
**Sugar:** You are not making it “sweet.” You are helping browning and balancing the dough. Even for savory choux, a little sugar is normal.
**Bread flour:** Higher protein = stronger structure = better rise. All-purpose will still work in a pinch, but bread flour gives you a little more forgiveness.
**Eggs:** Eggs are not just moisture. They are structure, sheen, and elasticity. The dough needs enough egg to be pipeable, glossy, and able to expand without tearing.

blocks.text: The Big Secret: Learn What “Correct Dough” Looks Like
Choux is one of those recipes where the exact number of eggs can vary slightly depending on how much moisture cooked off in the pan.
You want dough that is:

items: smooth and glossy
thick but pipeable
able to hold a peak that gently droops (not stiff like frosting, not runny like batter)

blocks.text: If you’re ever unsure, you are better off stopping slightly short than making it too loose. Too much egg = spread-out, flat puffs.
Step-by-Step Instructions
1) Make the panade (the cooked dough base)

items: In a 3-quart saucepan, combine water, milk, butter, sugar, and salt.
Bring to a full boil over medium heat.
Remove from heat. Add the flour all at once.
Stir vigorously until the mixture forms a smooth ball and pulls away from the sides of the pan.

blocks.text: **What you’re looking for:** no dry flour left, and the dough looks like one cohesive mass.
2) Dry out the dough

items: Return the saucepan to medium heat.
Cook, stirring frequently, until the dough feels dry to the touch.
If using an instant-read thermometer, you’re aiming for 165°F (74°C) to 175°F (79°C), about 3 minutes.

blocks.text: **Why this matters:** You are evaporating excess water so the dough can take the right amount of egg and still puff properly in the oven.
3) Incorporate the eggs

items: Transfer the dough to a food processor.
Process until the dough cools to 140°F (60°C) to 145°F (63°C), about 30 seconds.
With the processor running, slowly stream in the eggs.
Process until fully incorporated, about 20 seconds.
Stop and scrape down the sides and bottom.
Process again until smooth and homogenous, about 30 seconds more.

blocks.text: **If you don’t have a food processor:** Use a stand mixer with the paddle attachment. Beat the dough for a minute to cool it slightly, then add eggs gradually, mixing until glossy and smooth.
4) Rest the dough (so it pipes cleanly)

items: Transfer choux dough to a piping bag fitted with a 1/2-inch round tip or a closed star tip.
Refrigerate until firm to the touch and within 70°F (21°C) to 80°F (27°C), about 30 minutes.
If resting at room temp, plan for about 1 hour.

blocks.text: **Why rest at all?** Resting makes the dough easier to pipe cleanly and helps it hold its shape.
How to Pipe (Without Making It Weird)

items: Pipe straight down, not at an angle.
Keep the tip close to the tray so you don’t create “tails.”
If you do get little peaks, dab your finger in water and gently press them down so they don’t burn.

blocks.text: If you’re making gougères, a star tip gives you more surface area and crisp edges. For cream puffs, a round tip gives you that classic smooth dome.
Baking Notes (The Part That Makes or Breaks It)
This page is focused on the dough itself, but here are the baking rules that keep choux from collapsing:

items: **Bake hot enough to create steam quickly.** That steam is the lift.
**Do not open the oven early.** If you open the door before the shells set, they can deflate.
**Dry them out at the end.** Even after they’re browned, a few extra minutes helps evaporate moisture so they stay crisp.

blocks.text: If your puffs look beautiful but collapse as they cool, they usually needed more bake time to dry out.
Variation: Cheesy Gougères

Gougères are the savory, cheesy version: crisp outside, tender inside. They’re also an elite move for a date-night snack board. Wine, cheese puffs, a little music, and suddenly the night feels curated.

items: 150 g Gruyère, grated
After the eggs are incorporated, add the Gruyère and process until evenly mixed, about 30 seconds.

blocks.text: **Extra credit:** Add a pinch of black pepper or cayenne. Not enough to make it “spicy.” Just enough to make it interesting.
Troubleshooting (So You Don’t Panic)

items: **Dough is too stiff:** You likely cooked off a bit too much moisture. Next time, shorten the drying step slightly. You can sometimes fix it by adding a small amount of egg (a tablespoon at a time) until it becomes glossy and pipeable.
**Dough is too loose:** Too much egg. Next time, stop early and check consistency. Loose dough spreads instead of puffing.
**Puffs don’t rise:** Oven not hot enough, dough too wet, or you opened the oven too early.
**Puffs rise then collapse:** They weren’t baked long enough to dry out.

blocks.text: “During the Date” Notes
If you want to make pâte à choux feel like a whole moment:

items: Pipe and bake the shells earlier in the day.
Right before serving, crisp them for a few minutes in a low oven.
Fill them at the last second so they stay crisp.

blocks.text: Cream puffs that crunch lightly when you bite in? That is the kind of detail people remember.
Notes

items: Resting at 70–80°F makes the dough easier to pipe.
This recipe yields about 30 medium puffs.
